How Detectors Recognize a Type

detector-kinds.Rmd

A detector is a small function that looks at a column of values and answers one yes/no question: “is each value a such-and-such?” It takes a character vector and returns TRUE / FALSE for each value (and NA where the value was missing). formex ships dozens of them — is_date(), is_ein(), is_us_state(), and so on (the Data-Type Detector Guide is the full catalogue).

But detectors do not all work the same way. A date can be written a hundred ways, so its detector has to parse; a US state is one of exactly 51 things, so its detector just looks it up. This guide walks through the handful of detection kinds — the strategies detectors use — and shows, with real examples, what makes each one fire or stay silent. Understanding the kinds explains both why some columns are easy to recognize and why others are impossible to recognize from their values alone.

Every type in the ontology records its kind in a field called match_kind. There are six.

genome — parse it many ways

Dates and times have no single written form: 3/15/2019, 2019-03-15, and March 15, 2019 are the same day. A genome detector handles this by trying a whole library of formats and accepting the value if some format parses it into a real, in-range date that reads back consistently.

is_date(c("03/15/2019", "2019-03-15", "2019-13-45", "banana"))
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE

The first two fire — different writings of a valid date. The third does not: there is no 13th month or 45th day, so no format produces a real date. The fourth is not a date in any form. The detector is tolerant about style but strict about validity.

mask — match a fixed shape

Many identifiers have one rigid shape: an EIN is two digits, a dash, then seven digits. A mask detector checks that exact pattern. Some masks go further and validate a built-in check digit — an extra digit computed from the others, so a single typo is caught arithmetically.

is_ein(c("01-2345678", "12-3456789", "12-345"))
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE

The first two match the NN-NNNNNNN shape; the third is too short and fails. Now a check digit in action — an ISBN carries one, so a value with the wrong final digit is rejected even though its shape is perfect:

is_isbn(c("0306406152", "0306406153"))
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE

Same ten-digit shape, but only the first has a valid checksum. This is the tightest kind of recognition: the value essentially proves itself.

lexicon — look it up in a list

Some types are a closed set: there are exactly 50 states plus DC. A lexicon detector simply tests membership in a known list (matching case-insensitively).

is_us_state(c("CA", "tx", "ZZ", "California"))
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE

CA and tx are on the list; ZZ is not. Notice California fails too — this particular detector recognizes the two-letter abbreviation, not the full name (a different detector handles spelled-out names). A detector only knows what is in its list:

is_first_name(c("James", "Mary", "xzqwt"))
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE

James and Mary are in the reference list of common given names; xzqwt is not. Lexicon detectors are precise but only as complete as their list — a rare name that is not in it will be missed. That is a deliberate trade: better to stay silent than to guess.

mask+lexicon — the right shape and a real value

Some types need both: the shape has to be right and part of the value has to be in a reference list. A county FIPS code is five digits whose first two are a real state code — so a random five-digit number does not qualify.

is_county_fips(c("06037", "36061", "99999", "6037"))
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE

06037 and 36061 are five digits with valid state prefixes (06 = CA, 36 = NY). 99999 has the right shape but 99 is not a real state. 6037 is only four digits. Both halves must pass.

shape — the look of the numbers

Some columns cannot be recognized by any single value, only by the pattern of the whole column. “Is this a count?” is not something you can ask of one number — 42 could be a count, an age, a score. A shape kind looks at the column’s overall numeric profile (are the values whole? non-negative? bounded between 0 and 1?) to make a soft call. There is no single is_count() that fires on one value, because the signal lives in the distribution, not the digits.

none — not knowable from the values

Finally, some types simply cannot be recognized from values at all:

  • A membership-ID column is just integers — indistinguishable from any other integers.
  • A free-text notes column is just text.

These are marked none, and no detector claims them. They can only be asserted from outside the data — the column’s name, or a data dictionary. Being honest about this is a feature: it stops the engine from inventing a confident answer where none is possible.

From detectors to a guess

A single detector answers one question. To guess what a column is, guess_data_type() runs many detectors over a sample of the column and looks at the pass rate of each — the share of values it accepted. score_data_type() exposes that raw step:

score_data_type(c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020", "01/01/2021"))[1:4, ]
#>          data_type n pass_rate
#> 34         us_date 3         1
#> 49            date 3         1
#> 1    currency_code 3         0
#> 2  currency_symbol 3         0

Often more than one detector fires. A clean date column is accepted by both the US-date detector and the general date detector — both pass at 1.0. So a pass rate alone is not enough; the guesser needs a way to choose among the winners. It does this in two stages:

  1. A router proposes a short list of the most likely types for the column (using the detector signals plus a broader profile of the column — see the Feature Engineering for Type Guessing vignette).
  2. A verifier then re-runs each candidate’s full recipe and keeps only the ones that both fit the column and reject junk, breaking ties toward the more specific type.

The result is the $route — the type it settled on, reported only as far down as the evidence supports:

guess_data_type(c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020", "01/01/2021"))$route[
  c("semantic_type", "format_style", "match_kind", "depth", "confidence")]
#> $semantic_type
#> [1] "calendar"
#> 
#> $format_style
#> [1] "calendar"
#> 
#> $match_kind
#> [1] "genome"
#> 
#> $depth
#> [1] 4
#> 
#> $confidence
#> [1] 1

The match_kind in that answer tells you how the type was recognized — here, genome, because a date was parsed. A column recognized by lexicon would say so, and a column that only matched a none-kind type would never resolve to a leaf at all. In short: the detection kind is not just an implementation detail, it tells you how much to trust the guess and why.
